analysis|12-16|1991|Το Καζακστάν ανακηρύσσει την ανεξαρτησία του|Kazakhstan declares its independence|At the end of the 1980s the reform policy of Gorbachev opened the way to wider autonomy for the Soviet republics. Kazakhstan had particular issues, such as the nuclear tests at Semipalatinsk, which caused intense environmental and social reaction, and a multi-ethnic population with complex relations. The leader of the republic, Nursultan Nazarbayev, handled the path toward independence with care. // The dissolution of the Soviet Union was accelerated after the failed coup attempt in August 1991 and the secessions of the other republics. On 16 December 1991 the government of Kazakhstan proclaimed the state independence of the country, shortly before the final dissolution of the USSR. The proclamation was followed by international recognition, and the country began to shape its own institutions. // The independence of Kazakhstan is the largest in territory of the new states of Central Asia and marked a new geopolitical balance in the region. The country kept close ties with Russia, while it developed relations with Western countries, China and neighbouring states, especially because of its energy resources. Its historical significance lies in confirming the course of the post-Soviet states toward international autonomy.

analysis|12-17|1903|Οι αδελφοί Ράιτ πραγματοποιούν την πρώτη πτήση με κινητήρα|The Wright brothers make the first powered flight|At the end of the 19th century many scientists and inventors were trying to build a heavier-than-air craft with an engine and the capacity for controlled flight. The Wright brothers, who kept a bicycle workshop in Dayton, Ohio, had for years studied the mechanics of wings, the control of balance and the behaviour of airfoils. Their work was based on experiments, on a wind tunnel and on tests with gliders. // On 17 December 1903 Orville Wright flew their aircraft on a sandy stretch near Kitty Hawk in North Carolina, while Wilbur ran beside him. The first flight lasted about twelve seconds and covered a short distance, but it was the first controlled flight of a powered aircraft. Other, longer flights took place the same day. // The success of the Wright brothers was a milestone for aeronautics and opened the way for the development of aircraft in the 20th century. The control mechanisms they designed influenced later constructions. The significance of the flight is twofold: technological, since it showed that controlled flight was feasible, and historical, since it became a symbol of human effort to surpass limits. Their success is attributed to systematic methodology, measurement and the persistent testing of their ideas in the field.

analysis|12-17|1989|Πρεμιέρα των Σίμψονς|The Simpsons premieres|The series was created by Matt Groening, who already had known comic strips. The idea came from short sketches shown on The Tracey Ullman Show in 1987, and James L. Brooks and Sam Simon developed them into a full-length series. American television was then dominated by family sitcoms, and an animated series with satirical content was a relatively bold choice. // The premiere of the full series on the Fox network in December 1989 introduced the Simpson family, with Homer, Marge, Lisa and Bart, in a slightly satirical picture of American everyday life. The first episodes provoked discussion about the language, the unconventional humour and the presentation of the family as more imperfect than the usual television models. The audience response was gradually positive. // The series became one of the most important cultural phenomena of television. Its longevity, with many seasons, places it as the longest-running American animated series, and it influenced many later comedies with political satire and social analysis. As a symbol of pop culture it continues to be broadcast in many countries. The success of the series was recognized with many awards, among them Emmy awards connected with television creation.

analysis|12-17|1989|Ξεκινά η σειρά «Οι Σίμπσονς»|The Simpsons series begins|The animated series of Matt Groening arose from short sketches that had been presented in another programme at the end of the 1980s. The creators wished to carry family humour into a more complex form, with full-length stories and wider satirical themes. The choice of animation gave freedom to unconventional ideas that would be difficult to present with live actors. // The first episode of the full series was broadcast in the United States in December 1989 and showed an ordinary American family from an imaginary town, with characters who had flaws and everyday weaknesses. The series received criticism for its style, but the audience welcomed it positively, and its popularity grew over time. // The series of Groening became the longest-running American television series in the genre of animated comedy and was established as a cultural point of reference. With its satire of politics, religion and consumer culture, it opened the way for other series for adults. Its legacy is evident in many works of contemporary television. Its characters are recognized all over the world, and the series remains a subject of discussion for its social criticism.

analysis|12-18|1803|Ο χορός του Ζαλόγγου|The Dance of Zalongo|At the beginning of the 19th century the Souliot community, which lived in the mountains of Epirus, resisted the attacks of Ali Pasha of Ioannina, who sought to subdue it. After successive defeats and the fall of Souli, many Souliots sought refuge on neighbouring heights. The need to avoid capture in a difficult and dangerous situation led to dramatic choices. // According to tradition, women and children who had gathered at Zalongo, surrounded by the forces of Ali, preferred to throw themselves over the precipice rather than be captured. The women danced at the edge of the rock, singing, before throwing their children and themselves into the void. The account was transmitted mainly through oral testimonies and later records, and its details are discussed by historians. // The sacrifice of Zalongo became a symbol of resistance and honour in Greek historiography, literature and poetry, and it is depicted in works of art of the 19th century. Its historical significance is linked with the national memory of the struggles before the Greek Revolution. At the same time, historians stress the need for careful assessment of the sources, so that the historical basis can be distinguished from the romantic additions of the era.

analysis|12-18|1865|Η 13η Τροπολογία τίθεται σε ισχύ|The 13th Amendment takes effect|The American Civil War (1861-1865) broke out mainly because of disputes over slavery and over whether it would be extended to the new territories. Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation (1863) targeted the enslaved people in the states of the Confederacy and made the question a central aim of the war. However, with liberation only in certain areas, complete abolition required a constitutional amendment that would apply throughout the country. // Congress approved the 13th Amendment in January 1865, and then the required majority of states ratified it by the end of the same year. The official proclamation of its force was made on 18 December 1865, and in this way slavery was abolished throughout the territory. The process was complex and required a majority in both houses of Congress and ratification by three quarters of the states. // The abolition of slavery was an important step for individual rights, but it did not immediately end discrimination against African Americans. The following amendments, the 14th and the 15th, secured equality before the law and the right to vote, although their full implementation was delayed for decades. The 13th Amendment remains a foundation of American constitutional history and of the struggles for political equality.

analysis|12-18|1892|Πρεμιέρα του «Καρυοθραύστη»|Premiere of The Nutcracker|At the end of the 19th century Russian ballet was flourishing in Saint Petersburg, mainly at the Mariinsky Theatre. Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky had already written works such as "Swan Lake", and he was asked for music for a new ballet to accompany a performance suitable for the Christmas festivities. The story was based on the tale by E.T.A. Hoffmann and an adaptation by Alexandre Dumas. // The premiere took place in December 1892 and the performance received mixed reviews. The choreography of Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov stood out, and Tchaikovsky's music was regarded as impressive, while the plot was judged by some to be fragmentary. Later the music of the ballet became known also in the form of a suite for concerts. // The Nutcracker has today become one of the best-known works of the classical repertoire and is performed every Christmas around the world. Its music, with its characteristic motifs, influenced culture more widely, cinema and advertising. Its importance lies in having turned a work that had initially received a modest reception into an emblematic symbol of the festive season. Today the ballet is regarded as a cornerstone of the repertoire, and the scene with the snowflakes and Clara's journey remain among its most recognizable elements.

analysis|12-18|1958|Το πρώτο δορυφορικό μήνυμα|The First Satellite Message|After the launch of Sputnik by the Soviet Union in 1957, the United States accelerated its space programmes. The American agency wished to show that it could use satellites for communication and not only for scientific measurements. The SCORE programme was developed within this effort, to test telecommunication technologies from space. // On 18 December 1958 the SCORE satellite broadcast a recorded Christmas message from President Dwight Eisenhower, which had been recorded before the launch. The satellite transmitted the message when it was over certain areas, proving that voice radio broadcasting from orbit was feasible. It was a pioneering communication of this kind. // The success of SCORE was of great importance for the international profile of American space efforts, in a period of intense competition with the Soviet Union. The satellite communication that followed led to the development of telecommunication satellites, which today allow international television broadcasts, international telephony and part of world communications. The satellite operated for a few days and remains in history as the first example of radio communication broadcast from space. The test showed that a satellite could store messages and transmit them at a suitable moment, and this opened the way for the systems that followed.

analysis|12-19|1843|Εκδίδεται το «Χριστουγεννιάτικο Τραγούδι» του Ντίκενς|A Christmas Carol by Dickens is published|In the mid-19th century industrial Britain experienced great social inequalities, with poor working classes and inadequate measures of social protection. Charles Dickens, who had already become known through novels as a commentator on society, wished to raise public awareness of poverty and of the indifference of the rich. "A Christmas Carol" was written in a short time as a story with a moral message. // The story follows Ebenezer Scrooge, a miserly businessman who, through visits from three spirits, revises his attitude toward his fellow human beings. The book was published a few days before Christmas 1843, and its publication immediately gained great appeal. The rapid success was due to its emotional power and easy readability. // The work helped shape the modern image of Christmas, with emphasis on family, generosity and social solidarity. Its influence was enormous on popular culture, and the story has been adapted many times for the theatre and cinema. It is also regarded as an important example of how literature can influence public debate about social policy. The book was widely read and helped make the idea of the spirit of Christmas a common place of European and American culture.

analysis|12-19|1961|Η Ινδία προσαρτά τη Γκόα|India Annexes Goa|After India's independence from Britain in 1947, the Portuguese possessions of Goa, Daman and Diu remained under Portuguese administration. India considered that these territories should be incorporated into its state and asked for negotiations for their transfer. Lisbon refused to discuss the issue in substance, and the disagreement lasted for years. // On 19 December 1961 the Indian army entered the colonies, in an operation that lasted only a few days. The Portuguese forces, fewer and with limited means, surrendered within a short time, and the final result was the administrative incorporation of the territories into India. The operation was named Operation Vijay. // The annexation provoked international reactions, as the UN Security Council discussed the question, without however changing the outcome. For India, the incorporation meant the completion of the liberation of its territories from European colonialism. For Portugal, the loss was a blow to its prestige, and the dispute affected relations between the two states for decades. The operation provoked varied international reactions and divided international public opinion, while for the population of Goa the incorporation meant a significant change in administration, language and everyday life in the region.

analysis|12-20|1522|Οι Ιππότες παραδίδουν τη Ρόδο|The Knights surrender Rhodes|In the early 16th century the Order of the Knights of Saint John, also known as the Knights of Rhodes, ruled the island of Rhodes, which was a base for the defence of the eastern Aegean and of the Mediterranean against Ottoman expansion. The Knights had strong walls and castles, and their position was critical for control of the sea routes of the region. Their presence had for decades been a thorn for the Sublime Porte. // In 1522 Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent organized a large campaign with fleet and army, and the siege of Rhodes lasted about six months. The defenders resisted stubbornly, but shortages of men and supplies, together with exhaustion, led to negotiations. Finally, at the end of December, the Grand Master of the Order, Villiers de L'Isle-Adam, accepted the surrender on terms, and the Knights left the island. // The loss of Rhodes opened the way to Ottoman domination of the Aegean and strengthened the influence of the Sublime Porte in the Mediterranean. The Knights later moved their activity to Malta, where they settled in 1530. The siege and surrender of Rhodes are an important chapter in the relations of Europe with the Ottoman world and in the history of the island.

analysis|12-20|1803|Η Λουιζιάνα περνά στις ΗΠΑ|Louisiana passes to the US|In 1800 Spain had returned Louisiana to France, but Napoleon needed money for his wars and was interested in strengthening the French presence in America. The United States, which needed free access to the Mississippi River and the port of New Orleans, negotiated with France, and in 1803 agreed to the purchase of a vast territory. The agreement is known as the Louisiana Purchase. // On 20 December 1803 France officially handed over the region to the American representatives in New Orleans, in a ceremony that marked the completion of the transfer. The agreement included an area that roughly doubled the American territory, covering much of the present central region of the United States. The process was completed with the official signatures and the establishment of American administration. // The Louisiana Purchase radically changed the geography and economy of the United States, as it opened new areas for agriculture and trade. It also strengthened American expansion to the west, with serious consequences for the indigenous peoples who lived in those areas and for the question of slavery in the new lands. Its historical significance lies in having laid the foundations for the shaping of the modern American territory.

analysis|12-20|1860|Η Νότια Καρολίνα αποσχίζεται|South Carolina secedes|After the election of Abraham Lincoln to the presidency in November 1860, many Southern leaders believed that the new government would restrict slavery and endanger the economy of the southern states, which relied on plantations and the labour of enslaved people. South Carolina was one of the most strongly pro-slavery states, and its reaction was more immediate than that of the others. // On 20 December 1860 the convention of South Carolina approved the dissolution of its connection with the Union, making it the first state to secede. Other southern states followed, and in early 1861 the Confederacy was formed, with the result that the American Civil War began. The decision had the legal and political form of independence. // The secession of South Carolina was the beginning of a crisis that led to the Civil War and to the final abolition of slavery. The event showed that the question of slavery had reached a point that could no longer be resolved by political compromise. Its significance is twofold: it is the prelude to the conflict and evidence of the deep divisions of American society. South Carolina's decision soon influenced the stance of the other southern states, which followed the same course within the next few weeks.

analysis|12-20|1989|Οι ΗΠΑ εισβάλλουν στον Παναμά|The US invades Panama|At the end of the 1980s Panama was under the effective control of General Manuel Noriega, who had been linked with drug trafficking and with the repression of the opposition. The United States, which had military and economic interests in the region, and especially regarding the Canal, had begun to criticize its leadership sharply. The confrontation escalated during 1989. // On 20 December 1989 American forces invaded Panama in the framework of Operation "Just Cause", with the aim of overthrowing Noriega. The operation had significant losses, both for soldiers and for civilians, and Noriega surrendered to the American authorities a few weeks later. The government elected in 1989 took up its duties. // The intervention had varied consequences. For Panama it meant the restoration of democratic government, while for the relations of the United States with Latin America it continued the debate on the use of military force and on the principles of national sovereignty. The operation remains a point of reference in discussions about American interventions abroad. The intervention provoked intense debate at the UN and in regional organizations, where many countries condemned the use of force, while others considered it justified.

analysis|12-20|1999|Το Μακάο επιστρέφει στην Κίνα|Macau returns to China|The Portuguese presence in Macau began in the 16th century, and for centuries the area was a trading hub between Europe and China. After the agreement on Hong Kong, Portugal and China agreed on the return of the territory, in a process based on the principle of "one country, two systems". The agreement provided for the preservation of some institutions and of the city's way of life. // On 20 December 1999 the handover ceremony took place, through which Macau was transferred to China. Portugal thus ended its presence in Asia, which was its last colony in the region. The territory became a Special Administrative Region of China, with its own economic and legal distinctiveness for a certain period. // The return of Macau was part of the wider process of ending colonialism in Asia. For China it meant the completion of a territorial question that went back to earlier agreements, while for Portugal it ended a long historical presence. Macau continues today to have a special status, with intense economic activity, particularly in gambling and tourism. The transition took place smoothly, without major clashes, and Macau continued to function under its own laws and with its own judicial and economic organization.

analysis|12-21|1828|Ιδρύεται η Σχολή Ευελπίδων|The Evelpidon School Is Founded|After the founding of the Greek state, Ioannis Kapodistrias, as governor, sought to organize the administration and the army on the basis of modern models. The lack of trained officers was a great problem after the War of Independence, since many fighters had no formal military training. The need for systematic education was intense, and the new state was seeking institutions that would help it to stabilize. // On 21 December 1828 the Evelpidon Military Academy was founded at Nafplio, intended for the training of officers. The school tried to combine military and general subjects, with the aim of the professional readiness of future officers. Kapodistrias was assassinated in 1831, and the school continued to operate under the new political authorities. // The founding of the Evelpidon School had long-lasting significance, as it was among the first institutions of professional military training in the Greek state. The school became a basic centre for training officers who served in the wars of the 19th and 20th centuries. In this sense it symbolizes the effort of the newly formed state to build institutions based on knowledge and systematic education. The institution was linked with the organization of the Greek army and with the formation of a body of officers that would serve the new state.

analysis|12-21|1913|Δημοσιεύεται το πρώτο σταυρόλεξο|The first crossword is published|At the beginning of the 20th century the newspapers of the United States were seeking new kinds of content to attract readers, and puzzles and word games were particularly popular. Arthur Wynne, a journalist of British origin working in New York, developed the idea of a puzzle based on a grid of letters and clues. The idea was to combine vocabulary knowledge with logic and the finding of associations. // On 21 December 1913 the newspaper New York World published the first crossword puzzle, which was then called a "word-cross puzzle". The game had a diamond shape, and the squares had to be filled with words that matched the clues. The response of the readers was positive, and the genre soon achieved wide appeal. // The crossword developed into one of the most widespread types of game and vocabulary education in the world. Today it appears in newspapers, magazines and digital platforms, and many languages have their own crossword tradition. Its history shows how a small innovation in the press can acquire a lasting cultural influence. The publication of the puzzle is regarded as decisive for the shaping of the genre, and the rules of the crossword developed over the years into more complex and more varied forms.

analysis|12-21|1968|Εκτοξεύεται ο Απόλλων 8|Apollo 8 is launched|In 1968 the American space agency NASA was in intense competition with the Soviet Union for supremacy in space. The Apollo programme aimed at a Moon landing before the end of the decade, and earlier tests had confirmed the spacecraft's systems in orbit around the Earth. The next mission had to go one step further, with a crew that would travel to the Moon. // On 21 December 1968 Apollo 8 was launched with three astronauts, Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and William Anders, bound for the Moon. It was the first time that humans left Earth orbit and entered orbit around another celestial body. The spacecraft orbited the Moon and returned to Earth in the following days. // The mission laid the foundations for the Moon landing of the following year and showed that humans could travel safely to the Moon and return. The data collected helped in the planning of the later missions. The mission remains in history also for the images of the Earth, which inspired a collective awareness of humanity's planetary responsibility. The mission also had symbolic significance, as the three astronauts read passages from Genesis on Christmas Eve, which became widely known.

analysis|12-21|1988|Η τραγωδία του Λόκερμπι|The Lockerbie tragedy|At the end of the 1980s terrorism targeting aircraft was particularly intense, and investigations into international actions by state-supported groups were under way. Pan Am Flight 103 set out from London for New York and was later linked to an explosive device placed in a suitcase. The precise identification of responsibility was a long and complex process. // On 21 December 1988 the aircraft exploded over Scotland, near the town of Lockerbie, and the wreckage fell to the ground. 270 people were killed, among the passengers and residents of the town. The disaster left many families without their loved ones. // The tragedy led to a long legal process, with a special court that operated in the Netherlands. A Libyan agent was convicted in 2001, while Libya later acknowledged responsibility and paid compensation. The disaster is regarded as important for the history of aviation security and of international cooperation against terrorism. The investigation included extensive collection of evidence from the wreckage, which made it possible to reconstruct the course of the flight. The case also influenced the way airlines and governments address the risk of bomb attacks.

analysis|12-22|1944|Η πολιορκία της Μπαστόν|The siege of Bastogne|During the Battle of the Ardennes the German forces had surrounded the Belgian town of Bastogne, where American units were stationed, mainly of the 101st Airborne Division. The town was a junction of road networks, and its capture would facilitate the German advance to the west. The siege seriously hampered the defence of the Americans, who had limited supplies. // On 22 December 1944 the Germans demanded the surrender of the town by ultimatum. The commander of the American forces, General Anthony McAuliffe, replied with the word "Nuts", a short and ironic refusal that quickly became known. The defence of the town continued until reinforcements arrived and the roads were opened. // McAuliffe's phrase became a symbol of American endurance and composure in critical moments. The defence of Bastogne helped to contain the German offensive and to maintain the Allied positions. Its history confirms the importance of small units in the great battle, and it gave the town a special place in historical memory. The successful defence of the town helped to prevent the Germans from completely encircling the American forces in that area. The reinforcements that arrived afterwards changed the local balance.

analysis|12-22|1964|Η πρώτη πτήση του SR-71|The first flight of the SR-71|In the early 1960s the United States needed an aircraft that could fly at high altitude and at very great speed, so as to gather information over hostile areas without being easily detected. The design was based on new materials, such as titanium, which withstood high temperatures caused by friction. The programme was assigned to the Lockheed company and to the team of Kelly Johnson. // On 22 December 1964 the aircraft, known as the Blackbird, made its first flight in California, in the Palmdale area. The aircraft was designed to fly at speeds many times that of sound and at high altitudes, and it was one of the fastest aircraft of its era. // The SR-71 served for decades and established itself as a symbol of technological superiority in the field of reconnaissance aircraft. Its speed made it a difficult target for anti-aircraft systems, and the data it collected influenced military thinking. The aircraft was withdrawn from American service in 1990, and today it remains emblematic in the history of aeronautics. The mission of the aircraft required special pressure suits for the pilots and special specifications, because the aircraft heated up considerably at high speed. These specifications made it an impressive technical achievement.

analysis|12-22|1989|Πέφτει ο Τσαουσέσκου|Ceaușescu falls|Romania had been under the rule of Nicolae Ceaușescu since 1965, who strengthened authoritarian control through the Securitate and the cult of his personality. Economic crisis, deprivation and the repression of dissidents had created intense discontent. In 1989, as the changes swept across Eastern Europe, the confrontation reached its critical point. // Demonstrations broke out in Romania, first in Timișoara and then in Bucharest. On 22 December 1989 Ceaușescu tried to address a mass rally, but the protest broke out and the developments forced him to flee the capital by helicopter. The army sided with the revolution, and power changed hands quickly. // The fall of Ceaușescu completed the changes of 1989 in Eastern Europe and put an end to one of the most isolated and harsh dictatorships of the Cold War. The dictator was arrested and tried, and was executed a few days later, an event that caused discussion about the justice of the procedure. The Romanian revolution leaves a complex legacy for the transition to democracy. The execution of the Ceaușescu couple, on 25 December 1989, remained controversial, since many saw it as an act of justice and others as an incident that called into question the legitimacy of the process.

analysis|12-23|1913|Ιδρύεται η Ομοσπονδιακή Τράπεζα των ΗΠΑ|The US Federal Reserve is founded|At the beginning of the 20th century the United States faced repeated financial crises, such as the panic of 1907, which revealed the inability of the banks to stabilize the system. There was no central bank that could regulate liquidity, while the economy was fragmented among many local banks. The need for a central authority had become clear to politicians and businessmen. // President Woodrow Wilson signed on 23 December 1913 the law that founded the Federal Reserve System, known as the Fed. The law created regional banks under general supervision, with the aim of stabilizing the financial system and managing liquidity better. The design provided for cooperation between the public and the private sector. // The Fed became over time the most important institution of the monetary policy of the United States, influencing interest rates, inflation and employment. Its decisions have effects beyond its borders, since the American dollar is a basic international currency. Its founding marked the entry of the United States into a system of central management of monetary policy. The Fed has become a subject of public debate in every crisis, since its decisions affect the labour market, prices and the value of citizens' savings.

analysis|12-23|1947|Η πρώτη επίδειξη του τρανζίστορ|The first demonstration of the transistor|Until the mid-20th century electronics relied on thermionic valves, which were large, fragile and consumed a great deal of energy. Researchers at the Bell Laboratories were seeking materials that could amplify and control electric current without these disadvantages. The research team included physicists and chemists specializing in semiconductors. // On 23 December 1947 John Bardeen and Walter Brattain presented at the Bell Laboratories a circuit with a crystalline material capable of amplifying an electrical signal. William Shockley then developed the theory of the pn junctions, which led to more practical forms of the component. The device was named the transistor, and this discovery became the basis of future electronics. // The transistor gradually replaced valves and led to smaller, cheaper and more reliable electronic devices, from radios to computers. This development opened the way to integrated circuits and the digital age. The three researchers were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1956. The discovery was linked with long research on semiconductor materials and on the physics of junctions, and the competition among companies led to rapid industrial development and to new forms of components.

analysis|12-23|1968|Απελευθερώνονται οι ναύτες του Pueblo|The crew of the Pueblo is released|On 23 January 1968 the American intelligence-gathering ship USS Pueblo, lightly armed, was captured by North Korean forces in the open waters of the East Sea. North Korea claimed that the ship had entered its territorial waters, while the United States maintained that it was in international waters. The crisis intensified within the framework of the Cold War and the conflict in Asia. // The crew, about 80 men, suffered harsh treatment in captivity, and one sailor was killed during the capture. The negotiations lasted months, with the participation of international mediators. Finally, on 23 December 1968, the sailors were released after eleven months, while the United States signed a document of apology that at the same time denied the accusations. // The Pueblo affair revealed the tensions of the era and the limits of American military reaction. It became a subject of discussion about intelligence gathering in international waters and about the dangers faced by crews. The ship is today displayed as a museum in Pyongyang, and the affair remains a point of reference in American-Korean relations. North Korea continued to keep the ship, which is now displayed as a trophy. For the crew the experience of captivity remained deeply engraved, and the affair was examined by American committees for years.

analysis|12-24|1818|Εκτελείται πρώτη φορά το «Άγια Νύχτα»|"Silent Night" is performed for the first time|At the beginning of the 19th century Europe was going through social and economic changes, while religious music continued to play a central role in local communities. In Austria, the priest Joseph Mohr served in the parish of Saint Nicholas in Oberndorf, and the teacher and organist Franz Gruber worked with him on the music of the liturgy. The need was for a simple melody that was easy to perform. // On 24 December 1818 the church of Saint Nicholas heard the song for the first time, accompanied by a guitar, since, according to tradition, the church organ was broken. The text had been written by Mohr as a poem and Gruber wrote the melody. The simple composition moved those present and quickly became known in the region. // The song later spread across the world and was translated into many languages. "Silent Night" became one of the best-known Christmas songs, and today it is associated with the festive celebrations of many countries. Its history shows how a small work written for a local community can acquire worldwide appeal. The song was written in a simple form so that it could be performed by a few musicians, and this contributed to its rapid spread in villages and churches of the region.

analysis|12-24|1951|Ανεξαρτησία της Λιβύης|Independence of Libya|Libya had been an Italian colony since 1911, and after the Second World War the Allies administered the country. The question of its future was discussed in the United Nations, and the General Assembly decided that the country would become independent by early 1952. This decision was one of the first successes of the UN in managing decolonization. // On 24 December 1951 Libya was proclaimed an independent kingdom, with King Idris, leader of the national movement and member of the Senussi religious brotherhood, as its monarch. The country had limited resources and a small population, and its government rested on alliances with Western countries. // The independence of Libya was an important event for decolonization in Africa and in the Arab world. This monarchy lasted until 1969, when it was overthrown by a coup led by Muammar Gaddafi. Its significance lies in being one of the first applications of an international independence plan approved by the UN. The independence was accompanied by the establishment of a constitutional monarchy and the gradual organization of public institutions, while the revenues from oil, discovered later, gradually changed the economy. This development showed how important the international framework was for the new countries of the era.

analysis|12-24|1968|Η Γη βγαίνει πάνω από τη Σελήνη|Earthrise over the Moon|The Apollo programme aimed to land humans on the Moon, and Apollo 8 was the first mission that would reach lunar orbit with a crewed spacecraft. The mission was of great political significance, as the space race with the Soviet Union was at its height. The astronauts prepared for every detail of the flight. // On 24 December 1968 the astronauts Borman, Lovell and Anders photographed the Earth rising above the lunar horizon, an image that was called "Earthrise". The photograph was taken during the spacecraft's orbit around the Moon. The view of the Earth from such a great distance was unprecedented for humanity. // The photograph became one of the best-known images of the 20th century and contributed to awareness of the environment. It showed the planet as a fragile and unified space, without borders. Its symbolism influenced the movement for the protection of the planet and the ecological thinking of the following decades.
